name: Peak–end rule
statement: People judge a past episode by its most intense moment and its final moment, and take almost no account of how long it lasted.
meaning: The rule describes how an experience is compressed for storage. A colonoscopy, a film or a holiday is lived as hundreds of moments, and the retrospective verdict on it is well predicted by an average of two of them: the worst or best moment, and the last one. Everything in between is weighted lightly, and the number of moments is weighted close to zero. Two claims are bundled together here and they can come apart. The peak–end rule says which moments carry the verdict. Duration neglect, entry 262, says the length of the episode does not, and it is the older of the two findings. The practical consequence is that remembered utility and experienced utility diverge, so a person choosing which episode to repeat can choose the one that contained more total pain.

origin.who: Daniel Kahneman, Barbara L. Fredrickson, Charles A. Schreiber and Donald A. Redelmeier
origin.note: The cold-pressor paper names the pattern and tests it against a direct choice. Its companion, Fredrickson and Kahneman in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology four months earlier, established duration neglect with film clips and is the paper the 2022 meta-analysis credits for both ideas.

evidence: Thirty-two male University of California students, aged 19 to 39, held one hand in water at 14 °C for 60 seconds. On another trial they held the other hand in 14 °C water for 60 seconds, then kept it in for 30 seconds more while the temperature rose to about 15 °C. Three further subjects were run and replaced, one for a temperature-control fault and two for inconsistent choices. The long trial contained all the pain of the short one and then more. Told they would repeat one of the two, 22 of 32 chose the long trial, z = 2.15, p < .05 by sign test. The choice tracked whether the ending improved. Of the 21 subjects whose discomfort fell by 2 points or more, 17 chose the long trial, while the 11 who felt little or no relief split 6:5 for the short one. A version with the moment-by-moment discomfort meter removed found 24 of 37 choosing the long trial. On the rating scales most subjects said the long trial had caused less overall discomfort, M = -0.91, t(31) = 2.12, p < .05. Choice correlated .80 with that comparison of remembered discomfort and .16 with the comparison of durations. The pattern then held in a hospital. Redelmeier and Kahneman recorded real-time pain in 154 colonoscopy patients and 133 lithotripsy patients, and found remembered total pain correlated with peak intensity and with intensity over the last three minutes, both at P < 0.005, while long procedures were not remembered as worse. A 2003 randomised trial manipulated the ending. Of 733 patients approached, 682 agreed, and half of those had the colonoscope left resting in the rectum for up to three minutes. Mean pain over the final three minutes fell from 2.5 to 1.7 on a ten-point scale, P < 0.001, the global rating from 4.9 to 4.4 on a 10 cm scale, P = 0.006, and the ranking against seven other unpleasant events from 4.6 to 4.1, P = 0.002. In that trial the global rating correlated 0.56 with average pain across the whole procedure, above 0.44 for the peak and 0.33 for the final three minutes.

replication.headline: A meta-analysis of 174 effect sizes puts the peak–end effect at r = 0.581, and finds the plain average of the whole episode predicting just as well.
replication.detail: Alaybek and colleagues pooled 174 effect sizes and report the peak–end effect on retrospective evaluations at r = 0.581, 95% CI 0.487 to 0.661, robust across their boundary conditions and stronger than the effects of the first episode, the trough, the trend and the variability. It did not beat the average score across all episodes, which their abstract calls comparable. Duration came out essentially nil, so duration neglect survives the pooling as clearly as the peak–end rule does. The largest single test since is preregistered. Scharbert and colleagues took four experience-sampling samples, 2,035 people at intake and 1,889 after their exclusion rules, carrying 131,575 momentary measurements. They predicted retrospective well-being from the mean, the peak and the end of those measurements. For the general judgement the mean carried a standardised weight of .515, against .133 for the peak and .136 for the end, and adding the two moments moved the variance explained from .457 to .481. Both then faded with the wording. Asked about the past four weeks, N = 411, only the end reached significance at .101, p = .040. Asked to estimate their average response, N = 374, neither did. The failures cluster where the episodes are pleasant or long. Kemp, Burt and Furneaux collected 49 holiday records from 47 students, two of whom went away twice, on holidays averaging 7.5 days rated by daily text message. Recalled holiday happiness correlated .48 with the peak–end composite, against .64 with the average of the daily ratings and .63 with the happiness of the most memorable day. Peak happiness alone correlated .07, and holiday duration .06, so duration was neglected while the peak did no work. Mah and Bernstein tested 1,123 people across three experiments and analysed 988 of them, repeating Do, Rupert and Wolford's gift studies, in which a desirable gift followed by a less desirable one had been rated worse than the desirable gift alone. They found no such effect in preschoolers, school-aged children, or younger and older adults. Their first and largest experiment returned BF01 = 12, and a Bayesian meta-analysis across all three returned BF01 = 7.77 against the rule. Strijbosch and colleagues gave 40 Tilburg students a virtual-reality film and segmented it by what each viewer recounted. Peak valence predicted the immediate evaluation best, accounting for 41.9% of its variance, while end and peak–end valence were not significant. A week later the average across the whole episode won, at 46.2%.

study.cite: Alaybek, B., Dalal, R. S., Fyffe, S., Aitken, J. A., Zhou, Y., Qu, X., Roman, A., & Baines, J. I. (2022). All's well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 170, 104149.

limits: The 2003 trial is the weakest link in the popular account and its own paper says so. Its principal analysis was the rate of returning for a repeat colonoscopy, and on that measure the intervention did nothing: 53% against 48%, P > 0.20, which the paper puts as an 18% relative rise in the odds of returning, 95% confidence interval -13 to 59. The 41% increase in the odds of returning, 95% CI 2 to 96, P = 0.038, appears only after adjusting for prior colonoscopy, indication and abnormal findings, and the authors list under limitations that the difference was found only after that adjustment. The memory outcomes are the ones that came out clean. No effect size is printed here for the 1993 cold-pressor study. Its headline result is a choice proportion, and the correlations it does print describe choice rather than the size of a peak–end effect. The 1996 paper could not be obtained. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record it as closed, CORE and web search turned up no repository copy, and it is used here through its PubMed abstract. Its correlations of remembered pain with peak-and-end predictions, r = .67 for colonoscopy and r = .65 for lithotripsy, are quoted from Kemp and colleagues in 2008 and were not read off the 1996 paper. The 2022 meta-analysis is likewise paywalled. Its abstract was read in full at EconPapers, in the raw page and in a rendered fetch, and none of its moderator results are quoted. A 2024 corrigendum to it exists at Crossref and its content could not be obtained, the publisher blocking every route tried, so the figure above is the one published in 2022 and may since have been amended. Scharbert and colleagues are read from the accepted manuscript on PsyArXiv, the published version at the publisher being unreachable. Full text was read for the two 1993 papers, the 2003 trial, Do, Kemp, Mah and Bernstein, and Strijbosch. Searches for later work used a Crossref title search from 2022 onward and web search.
misreadings: The rule is repeatedly reported as showing that patients given a gentler ending came back for repeat colonoscopies more often. That was the trial's principal outcome and it was null before covariate adjustment. Duration neglect and the peak–end rule are also treated as one claim. They are separable, and Kemp's holiday study is the case that separates them: duration was neglected, correlating .06 with recalled happiness, while the peak carried nothing at .07 and the rule failed anyway. A third error is to reduce the rule to endings. It is an average of two moments, and the two terms fail separately. The peak carried nothing in Kemp's holidays, while the end dropped out of Strijbosch's film. A fourth is to treat the composite as the best available summary of an episode. Alaybek and colleagues found it no better than the plain average of every episode, and the 2003 trial's own data put average pain above both the peak and the ending. A fifth is to read the cold-pressor choice as uniform. It came from the subjects whose pain actually fell in the last 30 seconds, and those who felt no relief leaned the other way. The two 1993 papers are confused with each other, helped by both reporting 32 subjects: the film study used 32 Berkeley students, half of them women, and the cold-pressor study 32 men. The last error is scope. Every clean laboratory demonstration involves a short aversive episode, the attempts to carry it to gifts, holidays and immersive film have not found it, and where it does show up in everyday well-being it is small beside the average.
